title: Compass and Letter
premise: In 1893, Mara Dunmore, an apprentice clockmaker raised in an orphanage and taught to keep her head down, is hired to repair the great regulator clock of the Halvorsen Observatory. Inside its case she finds a sealed letter implicating the observatory's founding family in the disappearance of a cartographer whose maps were sold to a foreign navy. As the city's authorities close in, Mara and the observatory's ragtag household—a widowed astronomer, his deaf daughter, and a disgraced archivist—must smuggle the letter and the surviving map past three checkpoints to reach a parliamentary inquiry. Mara learns that history happened to her all along: the cartographer was her mother. The clock, repaired at last, strikes the hour of her testimony, and the family she found becomes the family history finally records.
about_author: Ulyana Underhill is a former museum conservator who spent a decade restoring maritime instruments before turning to fiction. She writes historical novels about the quiet people history overlooks, and lives near a decommissioned lighthouse with an unreasonable number of clocks.

chapters.title: The Hour That Stopped
chapters.summary: Mara Dunmore, POV. Summoned to the Halvorsen Observatory to repair its dead master clock, Mara arrives invisible as always, cataloguing her own smallness. She finds the great regulator jammed at 4:17, stopped for eleven years. Emotional beat: wary curiosity—the first time anyone has needed her hands for something that matters.

chapters.title: Household of Strays
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. She meets the observatory's odd residents: Astronomer Halvorsen, his deaf daughter Ingrid who reads lips through glass, and archivist Tomas Vey, dismissed in disgrace. They feed her supper unasked. Emotional beat: the strange discomfort of being welcomed when she has trained herself not to be.

chapters.title: What the Case Held
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Opening the clock's case to reach the escapement, Mara finds a sealed letter waxed to the frame, addressed to 'whoever keeps the time.' She almost leaves it. Emotional beat: dread—the moment invisibility stops being a shelter.

chapters.title: The Name in the Wax
chapters.summary: Tomas Vey, POV. Tomas recognizes the seal: the cartographer Lise Dunmore, who vanished in 1881 after her coastal charts were found in a foreign naval archive. The letter accuses the observatory's patrons of selling her out. Emotional beat: guilt, as Tomas admits he burned evidence once before.

chapters.title: Four Seventeen
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Mara realizes the stopped hour, 4:17, matches the time her mother supposedly drowned. She has spent her life believing history happened elsewhere; the clock says otherwise. Emotional beat: vertigo of identity, held tightly, half-denied.

chapters.title: The Patrons' Visit
chapters.summary: Astronomer Halvorsen, POV. The observatory's patrons arrive for a ceremony, and Halvorsen must smile while one of them, Aldous Crane, lingers by the clock. Halvorsen lies smoothly for the first time in years. Emotional beat: an old man discovering he still has something left to protect.

chapters.title: Ingrid Reads the Room
chapters.summary: Ingrid Halvorsen, POV. Deaf and sharp-eyed, Ingrid lip-reads Crane's threat through the window: the letter must not reach the inquiry. She warns Mara in the dark of the dome. Emotional beat: solidarity between two women who are always underestimated.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Tomas Vey, POV. Tomas maps the route to the parliamentary inquiry: the harbor gate, the customs house, the ministry stair. Each checkpoint requires papers none of them can forge well. Emotional beat: cold clarity—hope with a timetable attached.

chapters.title: The Escapement
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Mara works through the night repairing the clock, understanding that its chime at the inquiry hour could publicly timestamp the letter's arrival. The mechanism fights her. Emotional beat: craft as prayer; grief entering her hands through the gears.

chapters.title: What Tomas Burned
chapters.summary: Tomas Vey, POV. Tomas confesses fully: in 1881 he destroyed a page of Lise's logbook under pressure, and has kept the ash-stained remainder hidden. He gives it to Mara. Emotional beat: shame transmuted into restitution.

chapters.title: The Harbor Gate
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. First checkpoint: Mara hides the letter inside a delivery of clock weights, but a guard who once knew her from the orphanage hesitates—and lets her pass, saying her mother's name. Emotional beat: the past recognizing her before she was ready.

chapters.title: Crane's Offer
chapters.summary: Astronomer Halvorsen, POV. Crane offers Halvorsen funding, a restored reputation, and Mara's silence, wrapped in courtesy. Halvorsen refuses, and knows the observatory will pay for it. Emotional beat: costly integrity.

chapters.title: The Raid
chapters.summary: Ingrid Halvorsen, POV. Officials search the observatory while the household scatters the evidence; Ingrid hides the map fragments inside her chalkboard drawings, unread by men who assume silence means emptiness. Emotional beat: fury and triumph in one breath.

chapters.title: The Customs House
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Second checkpoint: a bribed clerk turns them away, and Tomas is detained. Mara must choose between the letter and the man. She sends the letter on with Ingrid and stays behind for Tomas. Emotional beat: found family made literal—no one left behind.

chapters.title: Night in the Holding Room
chapters.summary: Tomas Vey, POV. In custody, Tomas faces Crane directly and refuses, at last, to flinch. He hears Mara arguing for his release through the door. Emotional beat: an old coward's spine finally straightening.

chapters.title: The Broken Spring
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Freed by Halvorsen's intervention, Mara returns to find the clock sabotaged—mainspring snapped, hours before the inquiry. She must rebuild it from scrap with Ingrid's help. Emotional beat: desperation sharpened into focus.

chapters.title: Hands That Remember
chapters.summary: Ingrid Halvorsen, POV. Ingrid and Mara work in wordless rhythm, Ingrid feeling the clock's vibration for the beat Mara can't hear approaching. The mechanism turns. Emotional beat: two kinds of listening becoming one language.

chapters.title: The Ministry Stair
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Third checkpoint: Crane himself blocks the ministry stair, offering Mara her mother's real fate in exchange for walking away. Mara answers by stepping past him. Emotional beat: the quiet, total refusal of a person done being invisible.

Mara, POV. In the inquiry chamber the master clock, reinstalled and repaired, strikes 4:17 as Mara lays the letter, the map, and the scorched logbook before the commissioners. Her mother's name enters the record. Emotional beat: catharsis—the hour finally allowed to finish.

chapters.title: What the Record Says
chapters.summary: Tomas Vey, POV. The inquiry vindicates Lise Dunmore; Crane resigns rather than face charges. Tomas is offered his archive post back and declines, choosing instead to write the true account. Emotional beat: peace earned, not granted.

chapters.title: The Clock Keeps Time
chapters.summary: Ingrid Halvorsen, POV. The observatory reopens, and the household—Halvorsen, Ingrid, Tomas, Mara—keeps it running together, the master clock striking honest hours. Emotional beat: belonging, unremarkable and complete.

chapters.title: Compass and Letter
chapters.summary: Mara, POV. Mara visits the coastal cliff where her mother's charts began, carrying a compass Lise once owned and a letter of her own, sealed into the repaired clock for whoever keeps the time next. Emotional beat: memory as inheritance—history, at last, hers to hand on.
